title: RootLens: an incident-response lab that finds out why, then fixes it

scenes.title: RootLens: overview
lines: This is RootLens, my incident response lab.
When something breaks in production, it notices, works out why, and fixes it, but only within strict limits.
It's built with Python, FastAPI, Docker, Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry.

scenes.title: The problem
lines: Picture this. It's late at night, and a new release of the payment service goes out with a bug. Half of all customer orders start failing.
Normally, a human has to notice the alert, open the dashboards, guess which service is to blame, check what changed, and roll it back.
That takes minutes, sometimes much longer. RootLens automates that whole loop.

scenes.title: The five-step loop
lines: It runs the same five steps, every time.
Detect. Investigate. Decide. Act. And verify.

scenes.title: Architecture: 8 containers
lines: The lab is eight containers. Three FastAPI microservices form a small shop. The order service calls the user service and the payment service, with a three second timeout on each.
Each service has fault injection switches for errors and latency, and its v2 release contains a deliberately planted bug.
Prometheus scrapes every service every five seconds. Grafana draws the dashboards, and Jaeger collects OpenTelemetry traces.
A detector and a controller are the brains, and SQLite stores the incidents, deployments and an audit log.

scenes.title: Step 1: Detect
lines: Step one: detect. Every ten seconds, the detector asks Prometheus one question: what share of orders failed over the last minute?
If that ratio stays at or above thirty percent for three checks in a row, it opens an incident.
It only resolves after three healthy checks below ten percent. Two different thresholds mean an incident doesn't flicker open and closed.
The moment it opens, it captures evidence: each dependency's up metric, its own error ratio, how calls to it failed, the p95 latency, and recent deployments.

scenes.title: Step 2: Investigate
lines: Step two: investigate. For every dependency, the investigator scores three possible causes: it's down, it's returning errors, or it's too slow.
Each score comes from the evidence. If a service is up, failing more than twenty percent of its own requests, and its responses aren't slow, that points to errors.
Confidence is only high when the top cause scores at least 0.75, and beats the runner-up by at least 0.3.
It also works out the blast radius: which other services depend on the culprit.

scenes.title: What changed? Change correlation
lines: Then it asks the most useful question in any outage: what changed?
Every release is recorded. A release in the five minutes before detection counts as a strong link. Within fifteen minutes, a moderate one.
It even notices when the latest change was itself a rollback, so it never rolls back twice.

scenes.title: Step 3: Decide (the rulebook)
lines: Step three: decide. The rulebook is a pure function. It never touches Docker or the network, so every rule can be unit tested.
Only two actions exist: roll back a release, or restart a service. And only on the user or payment service, never the order service or its database.
It acts only with high confidence. If more than one service looks broken, it hands over to a human.
And it's rate limited: at most two attempts per incident, sixty seconds between attempts, and three actions per service per hour. Gentlest fix first: rollback, then restart.

scenes.title: Steps 4 & 5: Act and verify
lines: Steps four and five: act, and verify. The controller has three modes: off, dry run, and enforce. In dry run, it decides and records, but never acts.
In enforce mode, it first runs preflight checks. Is the incident recent? Is it still failing right now? Is the bad version still the one running?
Only then does the executor, the only code allowed to touch Docker, recreate the service on the previous version.
Then it verifies. Three healthy checks in a row means recovered. If not, it escalates to a human. And every decision, even choosing not to act, goes into an audit log.

scenes.title: Demo: a real incident
lines: Here's a real run. Payment service v2 ships at 12:25.
About a minute later, the failure ratio hits fifty two percent, and RootLens opens an incident.
The diagnosis: payment service is returning errors. Score one point zero, high confidence, and v2 was deployed sixty two seconds before detection.
The robot's decision: roll back payment service to v1.
After the rollback, three healthy checks later, the incident resolves by itself. The whole incident lasted under two minutes.

scenes.title: Tests & CI
lines: It's backed by a hundred and eighteen unit tests across six files: the investigator, the rulebook, the safety checks, the executor, the controller loop and the notifications.
GitHub Actions runs the tests, and builds every image, on every push.

scenes.title: Honest limits
lines: And the honest notes. The bug in v2 is deliberately planted, and this is a simulated release pipeline on one machine.
The write endpoints aren't authenticated yet. The controller mounts the Docker socket, which is fine on a laptop, but production would need narrower permissions.
And slowness that stays under the three second timeout isn't detected yet.

scenes.title: Recap
lines: Detect. Investigate. Decide. Act. Verify.
RootLens fixes things only within strict limits, and escalates when it isn't sure.
